title_full: Symphony No. 4 in B flat major, Op. 60

composer.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
composer.nationality_note: Grove calls him German. He was born in Bonn, then capital of the Electorate of Cologne, and lived in Vienna from 1792 until his death; no German state existed in his lifetime.

era_note: Kept Classical deliberately (decided 21 Aug 2026). periods.json buckets by year and the bucket sets the card colour; Romantic begins 1830, so all nine read Classical. The boundary is global, so moving it to split Beethoven would carry Haydn's late symphonies and the whole of Schubert across with him. Grove's three periods (first to c1802, second to c1812, third 1813-27) divide the nine 1-2 | 3-8 | 9, so the scholarly break falls at the Eroica, not at any date in the 1830s. Second period, but Haydnesque by design: a Romantic label would fit it worse than Classical does, whichever side of a date it fell on.

place.note: Wikipedia places the writing at Lichnowsky's Silesian estate, the commission arising from a September visit to Count Oppersdorff at Oberglogau nearby (Prussian Silesia, now Głogówek, Poland). Grove confirms 1806 and the Oppersdorff dedication but not the estate.

reason.summary: Commissioned by Count Oppersdorff, written at Lichnowsky's estate in Silesia.
reason.occasion: Oppersdorff kept a private orchestra and paid for a symphony after hearing Beethoven's Second played by it.
reason.detail: Grove quotes a letter to Oppersdorff revealing Beethoven's 'optimistic and resolute mood'. Grove also records the first performances: 'the Fourth Symphony and Fourth Piano Concerto were included at two concerts given at the palace of Prince Lobkowitz in March 1807, together with a new overture, to Collin's tragedy Coriolan.'

first_performance.notes: Grove: two private concerts at the Lobkowitz palace in March 1807, sharing the bill with the Fourth Piano Concerto and the new Coriolan overture. Wikipedia adds a first public performance at the Burgtheater in April 1808.

listen_for.hook: A slow, groping introduction in the dark before B flat major dawns.
listen_for.detail: Bernstein described a 'mysterious introduction which hovers around minor modes, tip-toeing its tenuous weight through ambiguous unrelated keys'.

listen_for.hook: Tovey thought this the work where he first mastered movement itself.
listen_for.detail: Grove quotes Tovey: the Fourth 'is perhaps the work in which Beethoven first fully reveals his mastery of movement'. Grove also notes, after Robert Simpson, that solid dominant–tonic resolution is withheld until the second theme of the recapitulation.

listen_for.hook: It sits between the Eroica and the Fifth, and gets overlooked for it.
listen_for.detail: Wikipedia notes the lighter instrumentation 'recalls the symphonies of Joseph Haydn' and that the two weightier neighbours have historically overshadowed it.

sources.title: Beethoven, Ludwig van
sources.author: Joseph Kerman, Alan Tyson, Scott G. Burnham, Douglas Johnson and William Drabkin

unknowns: Whether the whole symphony was written at Grätz; Grove does not name the estate at all.
